12760:
Priority means the state of being more important than something else, and therefore deserving attention, effort, or action first.

Think of it this way: you have a list of things to do, but you can't do them all at once. A priority is the thing on that list that gets to go first — because it matters more, because it's more urgent, or because ignoring it would cause the greatest harm.

Priority is always a relative concept. A thing isn't a priority in isolation — it's a priority compared to other things. It means: "Out of everything competing for my attention right now, this one wins."
Unpacking the Word

When something is your priority, three ideas are bundled together:

  1. Importance — It matters significantly. The outcome of this thing has real consequences.
  2. Ranking — It comes before other things. It sits higher on an invisible scale.
  3. Action — Because of 1 and 2, you give it your time, energy, or resources first.

So "priority" is not just about how much something matters in an absolute sense — it's about what you choose to handle before other things, given your limited time and resources.
Singular vs. Plural — A Subtle but Important Distinction

"Priority" (singular) implies there is one thing that matters the most above everything else.

"My priority right now is finishing this project."

Here, one thing reigns supreme. Everything else waits.

"Priorities" (plural) implies a ranked set of important things — a hierarchy where some things matter more than others, but several things still make the cut.

"My priorities this week are: passing my exam, resting, and calling my parents."

Here, there are multiple important things, but they are still ranked — the exam comes first, then rest, then the call.
High Priority vs. Low Priority

Not everything can be equally important. So when people have several things that need attention, they often speak of different levels of priority:

  • High priority — Needs to be done soon, or the consequences of delay are serious.
  • Low priority — Can wait. Less urgent or less important relative to other things.
  • Top priority — The single most important thing of all. Nothing else comes before this.

"Fixing the water leak is a top priority. Repainting the wall is a low priority."
When Both Urgency and Importance Matter

Two things often determine whether something becomes a priority:

  • Urgency: How soon does it need to happen? A deadline approaching fast creates urgency.
  • Importance: How significant are the consequences? A matter affecting health, safety, or a key relationship is important.

Something can be urgent without being truly important (a phone buzzing with a non-critical notification). Something can be important without being urgent (planning for retirement when you're young). But when something is both urgent and important — that's almost always a top priority.
Competing Priorities

Life often throws several important things at you at the same time. This is called having competing priorities — two or more things that each feel like they deserve your full attention, but you simply cannot give your full attention to all of them at once.

"I have competing priorities today — my boss needs the report by noon, and my child has a school event I promised to attend."

Dealing with competing priorities requires you to make a hard choice: which one matters more right now? That judgment — that act of ranking — is exactly what "priority" is about.
Setting Priorities

To set priorities means to consciously decide, ahead of time, what order you will handle things in. It's a deliberate act of ranking.

"Before starting her day, she set her priorities: health first, then work, then social obligations."

People and organizations set priorities so that when time runs out or resources are limited, the most important things have already been handled — and the least important are the ones left undone.
"Priority" in Different Areas of Life

The word is used everywhere, always carrying the same core meaning:

  • At work: "Customer safety is our highest priority." → It comes before cost, speed, or convenience.
  • In medicine: Doctors in an emergency room give priority to the most critical patients. They don't serve people in the order they arrived — they serve in the order of need.
  • In personal life: "Right now, my priority is my mental health." → Everything else gets less attention until this is addressed.
  • In government and policy: "Education is a national priority." → The government will allocate more funds and effort to it than to things ranked lower.
  • In technology: Computer systems assign priority levels to tasks so the processor knows which to handle first when it can't do everything simultaneously.

The setting changes. The meaning stays the same.
Common Phrases to Know

• Top priority — The single most important thing.
  • First priority — What gets handled before anything else.
  • High/low priority — Relative levels of importance.
  • Priority list — A ranked list of what matters most.
  • Set priorities — To decide what order things will be handled in.
  • Competing priorities — Multiple important things fighting for the same limited time or resources.
  • Make something a priority — To deliberately decide to give it more attention than other things.
  • Priority over — Used to express that one thing takes precedence above another. "Your health takes priority over your work."
The Deeper Truth About Priority

Here is what makes "priority" more than just a vocabulary word: it reveals what someone — or an organization, or a society — actually values.

People often say many things are important to them. But priority shows up in action: where you spend your time, your money, and your energy. If you say your health is important but you consistently work instead of sleeping, then work is your actual priority — revealed by your behavior, not your words.

In that sense, priorities are not just about planning. They are a mirror of genuine values.
One-Sentence Summary
A priority is something considered more important than other things, and therefore deserving of attention, effort, or resources before those other things.
12761:
Prissy means excessively proper, prim, and fussy — especially about things like manners, cleanliness, or correct behavior — in a way that is annoying or slightly ridiculous to the people around you.

The most important word here is excessively. Being polite and well-mannered is a good thing. But a prissy person takes it way too far, to the point where they become uptight, fragile, or insufferable about very ordinary situations.
What Prissy Looks Like in Real Life

A prissy person tends to:

  • Get easily shocked or offended by things most people find normal — a crude joke, a messy room, someone eating sloppily, or casual language.
  • Be overly fussy about small, trivial details — they won't sit on a chair if it has a speck of dust, or they refuse to eat food if it's not plated neatly.
  • React dramatically to anything that feels "beneath" their standards, often with a little gasp, a disapproving look, or a haughty sniff.
  • Avoid anything messy, rough, or uncomfortable — physically or socially. They don't want to get their hands dirty, literally or figuratively.
  • Come across as slightly self-righteous, as if they believe their high standards make them better than everyone else.

Think of a child who refuses to play in the mud because it's dirty, or an adult who wrinkles their nose at street food and insists on only "proper" restaurants. That fussy, delicate, too-good-for-this attitude is prissy.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Prissy is a mildly negative, critical word. When you call someone prissy, you are not complimenting them. You are gently (or not so gently) mocking them for being too delicate, too uptight, or too prim for their own good.

There's a faint sense of weakness in the word too — a prissy person seems unable or unwilling to handle anything rough, imperfect, or indelicate. They need the world to be sanitized and proper at all times.

The word often carries a slightly amused, slightly exasperated feeling. People use it when they find someone's overly proper behavior a bit absurd.
Who or What Can Be Called Prissy

People: Most commonly, the word describes a person. "She's too prissy to ever camp outdoors." "He's a bit prissy about his clothes — he irons his socks."

Behaviour or attitude: "That prissy attitude of hers drives everyone up the wall." "Stop being so prissy about it."

A manner or gesture: "He gave a prissy little wave of his hand and walked away." "She let out a prissy little gasp."

Note that while prissy can technically be applied to anyone, it has historically been used more often about men or boys to suggest they are being unmanly or too soft — though today it applies freely to anyone who fits the description.
The "Too Far" Factor — What Makes It Prissy and Not Just Polite

This is a crucial distinction. Consider:

  • Washing your hands before eating = normal, healthy, polite. ✓
  • Refusing to eat at a restaurant because the tablecloth has a tiny stain and demanding to leave = prissy. ✗
  • Disliking very crude jokes = a perfectly reasonable preference. ✓
  • Dramatically clutching your chest and leaving the room because someone made a mild off-colour comment = prissy. ✗

The line is crossed when the fussiness becomes disproportionate, inconvenient to others, or simply unnecessary. Prissy behaviour is never just about having good standards — it's about having standards so inflated and so rigidly enforced that they become a burden or a performance.

• "Don't be so prissy — it's just a little rain. We're not going to melt."
  • "She was too prissy to try the local market food, so she missed the best meal of the trip."
  • "He gave a prissy little sniff and said, 'I simply cannot work in a cluttered space.'"
  • "Stop acting so prissy and just help us move the furniture."
  • "The new manager has a rather prissy attitude about everything — he even complained that someone left a mug on the wrong shelf."

• It does not simply mean "polite" or "well-mannered." Politeness is respected; prissiness is gently mocked.
  • It does not mean mean-spirited or cruel. A prissy person is annoying, not malicious.
  • It does not mean shy or introverted. A prissy person can be quite vocal and expressive — often about how offended or bothered they are.

Ask yourself: Is this person being reasonably proper, or are they making everyone around them uncomfortable with their excessive, fussy, over-the-top standards?

If it's the latter — that's prissy.
12762:
Pristine describes something that is in a perfect, unspoiled state — either because it has never been touched or harmed, or because it has been cared for so well that it still looks and feels exactly as it did when it was brand new.

Think of it as the opposite of worn, dirty, polluted, or damaged.
The two main ways it is used

1. In nature: untouched and unspoiled by humans

When "pristine" describes a natural place, it means the place has not been polluted, developed, or altered by human activity. It exists in the same pure, original condition that nature created it in.

  • "They discovered a pristine forest where no roads had ever been built."
  • "The remote island had pristine beaches with crystal-clear water and no litter anywhere."
  • "Scientists rushed to study the pristine coral reef before pollution could reach it."

In these cases, "pristine" essentially means: "This place is exactly as nature made it — untouched, clean, and pure."

2. For objects and spaces: flawlessly clean and like new

When "pristine" describes an object, a room, or a space, it means the thing is in perfect condition — spotlessly clean, with no scratches, stains, damage, or signs of wear. It looks as perfect as the day it was made.

  • "The collector was selling a comic book in pristine condition — no creases, no yellowing, no marks whatsoever."
  • "She kept her kitchen pristine; every surface gleamed and nothing was ever out of place."
  • "He pulled a pristine white shirt from the drawer — not a single wrinkle or stain on it."

In these cases, "pristine" means: "This is in flawless shape — it looks brand new."
How "pristine" is different from similar words

Understanding the gap between "pristine" and nearby words will help you use it precisely.

Pristine vs. clean: "Clean" simply means free from dirt. Your hands after washing are clean. But "pristine" means far more — it implies a level of purity and perfection that is almost remarkable. After a car wash, your car is clean. But a car is pristine if it has been cared for so perfectly that it looks like it just rolled out of the factory — not a scratch, not a smudge, not a speck.

Pristine vs. new: "New" just means something was made recently. But something pristine may actually be quite old — it just looks new because it has been so well preserved. A 60-year-old watch can be in "pristine condition" if it has no scratches, no rust, and still runs perfectly.

Pristine vs. pure: "Pure" is mostly used for substances — pure water, pure gold, pure air. "Pristine" is broader and describes the overall state or condition of a place or object, not just its chemical makeup.

Pristine vs. immaculate: These are the closest synonyms, and you can often swap one for the other. The small difference is that "immaculate" focuses on spotless cleanliness or flawlessness, while "pristine" carries an added sense of being unspoiled or untouched — as if nothing has ever had a chance to damage it. A room can be immaculate because someone cleaned it perfectly. A room is pristine when it feels like no one has ever disturbed it.
The tone and feeling the word carries

"Pristine" is not a neutral word. It quietly carries a tone of admiration and wonder. When you call something pristine, you are not just observing — you are expressing that you are genuinely impressed. You are saying: "This is remarkable. It has managed to stay pure and perfect, and that is not easy."

This is why "pristine" tends to appear around rare or special things: a centuries-old manuscript that survived without a tear, a remote wilderness that industry never reached, or a vintage car that still looks showroom-fresh after 40 years. The word whispers: "This is special precisely because it hasn't been spoiled."

Do not use "pristine" for ordinary, everyday cleanliness or for something that is simply new. If you washed your dishes, they are clean — not pristine. If you just bought a pen, it is new — not pristine. Reserve "pristine" for moments when the level of purity or unspoiled perfection is genuinely striking and noteworthy.

"Pristine" also stays in the physical world. It describes places, objects, environments, and spaces. You would not use it for personalities, emotions, or abstract ideas. Saying someone has a "pristine personality" would sound odd and incorrect.
The full picture in one sentence

Pristine means in a state of perfect purity — either untouched by human damage (in nature) or flawlessly clean and preserved (in objects and spaces) — and it always carries an undercurrent of admiration, because truly pristine things are rare.
12763:
The word private describes something — a thing, a place, a piece of information, or a feeling — that is not open to everyone. It belongs to, or is meant for, only a specific person or a specific group. Everyone else is excluded, either by rule, by choice, or by social understanding.

The clearest opposite of private is public — which means open to all, available to everyone, or belonging to society as a whole. Keep this contrast in mind as you read through the meanings below, because it will make everything click naturally.

1. Belonging to a specific person or group, not to the public

When something is private, it means other people do not have the right to access it, use it, or enter it unless the owner allows them.

  • Private property — land or a building owned by someone. You cannot walk onto it freely.
  • A private parking space — reserved for one person; others may not use it.
  • A private club — only members can enter.

The key idea here: ownership or membership creates a boundary. Being private means that boundary exists.

2. Not shared with others; kept secret or confidential

When information, a conversation, or a feeling is private, it means it is not meant to be known by others outside a certain circle.

  • A private conversation — meant only for the people involved; no one else should be listening.
  • Private information — details about someone that they have not chosen to share publicly (their salary, their medical condition, their personal struggles).
  • Private thoughts or feelings — emotions and opinions that someone keeps inside and does not express to others.

Here, private means confidential or personal in a guarded way. If someone shares your private information without permission, it is considered a serious violation of trust — it is called a breach of privacy.

3. Secluded; away from other people

A place can be described as private when it gives you the feeling of being alone, unobserved, or undisturbed.

  • A private corner of the garden — tucked away, where no one can easily see or disturb you.
  • A private beach — a stretch of beach where the public is not allowed, so it is quiet and exclusive.
  • Can we find somewhere more private to talk? — meaning, a place where others cannot overhear us.

The feeling this meaning carries is peace, seclusion, and the absence of unwanted observers.

4. Not run by the government; independent

This is one of the most important and commonly used meanings, especially in everyday life and news.

When something is private, it is not owned, controlled, or funded by the government. Instead, it is owned by individuals or companies.

  • A private school — a school that is funded by fees paid by students' families, not by the government. Contrast: a government school or state school.
  • Private healthcare / a private hospital — medical services you pay for yourself, run by a company, rather than being provided free by the state.
  • A private company — a business owned by individuals or investors, not by the government. This also has a more specific financial meaning: a private company is one that has not sold its shares on a public stock exchange, meaning ordinary people cannot easily buy or sell a stake in it.
  • The private sector — the part of the economy made up of businesses and organisations not owned by the government. Its opposite is the public sector (government departments, state-run hospitals, public schools, etc.).

This meaning often carries a sense of choice, exclusivity, and independence from the state, though it also frequently means you must pay for the service yourself.

5. Separate from one's public life or professional role

People who hold public roles — politicians, celebrities, executives — have two sides to their existence: the part they show the world, and the part that belongs only to them personally. The second part is called their private life.

  • His private life is very different from his political image.
  • She keeps her family completely separate from her professional work — her children are part of her private world.
  • In his private moments, he is reportedly very funny, though his public persona is serious.

Here, private means personal, away from one's public or professional identity. Even public figures are generally thought to deserve some private space — things that belong to them as human beings, not as public figures.

6. Describing a person who keeps to themselves

When we say someone is a private person, we mean they are reserved — they do not easily share their feelings, personal details, or inner life with others. They are not secretive in a suspicious way; they simply prefer to keep to themselves.

  • She is a very private person and rarely talks about her family.
  • He is known for being private; interviews with him are rare.

This is a personality trait, not a flaw. It simply means the person places a high value on keeping their inner world to themselves.

In private — This phrase means away from other people, not in front of others. "Can I speak with you in private?" means: away from others, just the two of us. Compare to in public, which means in front of others.

Private parts — A polite, indirect way of referring to the genitals (the sexual organs of the body). This is a euphemism — a softer word used instead of a more explicit one.

Private detective / private investigator (P.I.) — A detective who works independently, hired by individual clients (not by the police or government) to investigate matters such as missing persons, cheating spouses, or corporate fraud.

Private eye — An informal term for a private detective.

Private practice — When a doctor, lawyer, or other professional works independently for individual paying clients, rather than working for a hospital, government body, or large institution. "She left the NHS and went into private practice."

A private matter — Something personal that should not be discussed with others or brought into public spaces.

Private label / private brand — Products made by a manufacturer but sold under a retailer's own brand name (common in supermarkets).
Why the Same Word Covers So Many Situations

You might wonder why one word — private — handles ideas as different as a beach, a school, a feeling, and a person's personality. The answer is the single thread running through all these uses:

Private = not open or accessible to everyone; restricted to a defined person, group, or space.

Whether it's a private beach (physically restricted), private information (socially restricted), a private school (institutionally independent from government), or a private person (emotionally restricted in what they share) — in every case, there is a boundary that separates the private thing from general, unrestricted access. The nature of the boundary changes (a gate, a secret, a fee, a personality), but the logic is identical.

It helps to see private on a spectrum opposite public:

  • A public park is open to all → A private garden is for the owner only.
  • A public hospital is run and funded by the government → A private hospital is run by a company, paid for by patients.
  • A public statement is shared openly → A private remark was not meant for others to hear.
  • A public figure lives much of their life in front of others → A private person guards their inner world.
  • In public means with others around → In private means away from others.

Whenever you encounter the word private, ask yourself: Who is being excluded from access, and why? That question will lead you to the correct meaning in any context.
12764:
Privation means the state of being without the things you need to live a decent, dignified human life — things like food, clean water, warmth, shelter, clothing, and safety. It describes a condition of severe, painful lack. When someone is suffering privation, they are not merely going without something they want — they are going without something they fundamentally need.

Think of it this way: if you skip dessert, that is not privation. If you have nothing to eat for days, that is privation.

The word carries weight. It is not a neutral or casual word. It implies real suffering, hardship, and often a prolonged struggle. When writers and historians use it, they are signaling that the conditions they are describing were genuinely harsh — not just uncomfortable, but painful and grinding.

A soldier enduring a freezing winter campaign with no food, no dry shelter, and no warm clothing is suffering privation. A refugee family with no access to clean water, medicine, or safety is living in privation. The word communicates that human beings are being denied what they rightfully need.

You will very often see this word used in the plural — privations — rather than the singular. This is because suffering of this kind usually comes from many losses at once: no food and no warmth and no shelter and no medicine. The plural form captures the idea that multiple necessities are missing at the same time.

"The prisoners endured terrible privations during the long winter." — This tells you they lacked many things at once.

The singular form, privation, tends to refer to the overall condition or state of lacking. "A life of privation" means a life lived in persistent deprivation of basic needs.
How it differs from similar words

Privation is close in meaning to several other words, but it is not quite the same as any of them.

Deprivation is the most similar word. The difference is subtle but real. Deprivation often suggests that something has been taken away from someone — there is an implied cause or agent doing the removing. "Sleep deprivation" suggests someone or something has caused you to lose sleep. Privation, by contrast, tends to describe the raw state of lacking, often as a result of circumstance, poverty, war, or disaster, without necessarily pointing a finger at who caused it. However, in everyday language, the two words overlap a great deal, and many people use them interchangeably.

Poverty refers specifically to a lack of money and material wealth. Privation is broader — it refers to the actual lived experience of going without necessities, which poverty can certainly cause, but privation is about the human experience of the lack itself, not just the economic category.

Hardship is broader still. Hardship covers any form of difficulty or suffering — emotional pain, grueling work, difficult circumstances. Privation is specifically about the absence of basic necessities. All privation is a form of hardship, but not all hardship is privation.

Want (as a noun) is an older, more literary word that means roughly the same thing — a painful lack of necessities. "In want" means lacking the basics of life. Privation is slightly more formal and powerful in tone, and more common in serious historical or literary writing.

In philosophy and theology, privation has a more abstract technical meaning: it refers to the absence of something that ought to be there — a missing quality in something that naturally should have it. For example, blindness is sometimes called the privation of sight (sight is something eyes are meant to have; its absence is a privation). In this tradition, darkness is the privation of light. Some philosophers have even argued that evil is the privation of goodness — not a positive force in itself, but the absence of good where good should exist.

You are far more likely to encounter privation in its everyday sense than this philosophical one, but it is worth knowing this layer exists, especially if you ever read older philosophical or religious texts.
Where you will typically encounter this word

Privation appears most often in serious, formal, or literary writing — historical accounts of wars, famines, or extreme poverty; literary fiction set during periods of hardship; journalism covering humanitarian crises; philosophy and theology. It is not a word you would normally use in casual conversation. Saying "I'm suffering privation because the café ran out of my favorite coffee" would sound absurd and dramatic. The word is reserved for genuine, serious human suffering caused by lack of what is essential.
A simple summary to anchor it all

Privation = the state of painfully lacking the basic necessities of life. It is serious, it implies real suffering, and it almost always refers to conditions that no human being should have to endure.
12765:
A privilege is a special advantage, right, or benefit that belongs to a particular person or group — but not to everyone.

Think of it this way: if everyone gets something, it is a basic right. But if only some people get it, it is a privilege.

That exclusivity — the fact that not everyone has it — is the heart of the word.

Imagine a school canteen. All students wait in a long queue to buy lunch. But the class prefects get to skip the queue and go straight to the front.

Skipping the queue is a privilege — it is a special benefit given to only a select group (the prefects), not to every student.
The Two Broad Ways "Privilege" Is Used

1. Privilege as Something Formally Granted

Here, a privilege is an official, specific advantage that someone is given by an authority — a government, an institution, a company, or a rule. It is deliberate and usually documented.

  • A member of a club enjoys membership privileges — discounts, early access, or entry to restricted areas.
  • A lawyer and their client share attorney-client privilege — a legal rule that protects their private conversations from being revealed in court.
  • A diplomat enjoys diplomatic privilege — protection from being arrested or prosecuted in a foreign country.
  • A paid subscriber gets premium privileges — features that a free user simply does not have access to.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: someone in authority decided that a certain group gets a certain advantage that others do not.

This type of privilege can usually be granted and taken away. If you misbehave in a prison, you lose visiting privileges. If your membership expires, you lose your membership privileges.

2. Privilege as an Unearned Social Advantage

This is the broader, more modern use of the word — particularly in social, political, and cultural discussions.

Here, privilege refers to advantages that certain groups of people are born into or grow up with, simply because of who they are — their race, gender, wealth, religion, nationality, family background, physical ability, and so on. These advantages were not earned. They are not formally written in any rulebook. But they are very real in everyday life.

Examples:

  • A person born into a wealthy family may have access to better schools, better food, better healthcare, and better social connections — simply because of the family they were born into. That is class privilege (also called wealth privilege).
  • In many societies, men have historically faced fewer automatic barriers in workplaces, courts, and public life than women have. That set of automatic, background advantages is referred to as male privilege.
  • In a society where the majority group's culture, history, and appearance are treated as the "default" or "normal," members of that majority group move through life without facing certain obstacles that minority groups regularly face. This is called majority privilege (e.g., white privilege in societies where white people are the dominant racial group).
  • A person who was born without a physical disability can enter most buildings, use most transport, and navigate public spaces without a second thought. That effortless ease of movement is a form of able-bodied privilege.

The key insight in this use of the word is: having a privilege does not mean your life is easy or free of hardship. It simply means that that particular thing is not one of the obstacles working against you.

A wealthy person may still struggle with illness, heartbreak, and failure. But their wealth means that money is not an extra obstacle on top of all the others. That is the privilege.
Privilege vs. Right — What Is the Difference?

This distinction is important.

A right is something that everyone is entitled to, simply because they are a person. It is universal and should not be taken away.

A privilege is something that only some people have access to. It is not universal.

RightPrivilege
Who has it?EveryoneA specific person or group
Is it universal?YesNo
Can it be taken away?Ideally, noOften, yes

For example:

  • The right to a fair trial is (ideally) a right — every person deserves it.
  • A VIP seat at a concert is a privilege — only those who paid extra or were invited get it.
"It Is a Privilege" — The Polite, Grateful Use

You will often hear people say things like:

  • "It's a privilege to meet you."
  • "I consider it a privilege to serve this community."
  • "Going to university was a privilege I didn't take for granted."

Here, the word is being used to express genuine gratitude and humility. The speaker is acknowledging that what they have, or what they are experiencing, is not something everyone gets — and they feel fortunate for it. This is a warm, positive use of the word.
Privilege Can Be Visible or Invisible

One of the most important things to understand about privilege — especially the social kind — is that it is often invisible to the person who has it.

This is because privilege works by removing obstacles. When you do not face a certain obstacle, you often do not notice its absence. You just... move forward. But someone without that privilege hits a wall where you sailed through — and they feel it clearly.

A fish does not notice the water it swims in. A person with a privilege often does not notice the privilege, because it simply feels like "normal life." But someone without it notices the difference very clearly.

This is why talking about privilege can sometimes feel uncomfortable to those who have it — it requires them to notice something they have never had to think about before.

AspectExplanation
What it isA special advantage, benefit, or right that not everyone has
Key featureIt is exclusive — it applies to some, not all
Formally grantedGiven by an authority; can be taken away
Social privilegeUnearned advantages from factors like birth, race, wealth, gender
vs. a RightA right is universal; a privilege is not
Often invisibleThose who have it may not notice it; those without it feel its absence
Grateful use"It's a privilege" = I'm lucky and grateful for something not everyone gets

The word "privilege" is one that can be used casually ("VIP privileges"), legally ("attorney-client privilege"), or in deep social discussions ("white privilege"). But no matter the context, it always comes back to the same idea: an advantage that belongs to some, but not all.
12766: "Privileged" describes someone or something that has a special advantage, right, or benefit that most other people do not have. Think of a privilege as a bonus — something extra that puts you in a better position than the average person. "Privileged" is the adjective form: it simply describes whoever or whatever holds that advantage.

1. Having more advantages in life than most people

This is the most common, everyday meaning. A privileged person has had life easier than most — usually because of wealth, family background, education, social class, race, or similar factors. Crucially, these advantages are often not earned. They come from circumstances the person was born into or inherited.

"She had a privileged upbringing — private schools, summers abroad, and family connections in every industry."
"He has never had to worry about money. He's very privileged."
"Growing up in a privileged household, she was unaware of how much others struggled."

Because these advantages are unearned, the word sometimes carries a gentle criticism — a suggestion that the person benefited from something they didn't work for, and may not even notice.

2. Having officially granted, special access or rights

"Privileged" can describe someone who has been formally given access to something that is not available to everyone — like a restricted area, a database, or confidential meetings.

"Only privileged employees are allowed into the data centre."
"The journalist had privileged access to the prime minister's private briefings."
"A small group of privileged users got to test the software before anyone else."

This meaning is mostly neutral. It simply means "specially authorized."

3. Legally protected and confidential

In law and formal professional settings, "privileged" means protected from being shared or disclosed — especially by law. A privileged communication or privileged document is one that cannot be forced into the open, even in a court case.

The most famous example is attorney-client privilege: whatever you say to your lawyer in confidence is "privileged." Your lawyer legally cannot be made to reveal it.

Other professions — therapists, doctors, clergy — may also operate under similar protections.

"This conversation is privileged. Nothing you say here can be used against you in court."
"The emails were marked 'privileged and confidential' and were protected from disclosure."
"What you tell your therapist is privileged information — they cannot share it without your consent."

This sense is about legal protection and restricted disclosure — not about social or economic advantages.

4. Feeling specially honored or fortunate

When someone says "I feel privileged to...", they are not claiming to be wealthy or socially advantaged. They mean: "I feel honored, lucky, or specially fortunate to have this opportunity." This is a more personal, emotional use of the word.

"I feel privileged to have known such a remarkable person."
"We are privileged to have Dr. Mehta with us this evening."
"It was a privileged moment — very few people ever get to witness something like that."

This sense is almost always positive and sincere. The speaker is expressing deep appreciation for something they consider rare or special.
The Tone and Connotation — Can Be Positive, Neutral, or Critical

One of the most important things to understand about "privileged" is that its emotional tone depends entirely on context.

Neutral: Simply acknowledging that someone has advantages, without judgment.

"She came from a privileged background."

Positive and warm: Expressing gratitude or honor.

"I feel truly privileged to be here."

Critical or challenging: Pointing out that someone has unfair advantages they benefit from but may be unaware of.

"He doesn't understand what it's like to struggle. He's privileged."

In modern social and political discussions, "privileged" is often used to talk about systemic advantages — benefits that come from factors like race, gender, social class, or physical ability. Someone might be called "economically privileged," "racially privileged," or simply "privileged" to mean that the system has been working in their favor, even if they never consciously noticed it. This is not always an accusation of being a bad person — it is often just an observation that life has placed fewer obstacles in their path than it has for others.

When you add the prefix "under-", you get underprivileged, which means having significantly fewer advantages than most people — lacking resources, opportunities, or access that others take for granted.

"The organization provides meals for underprivileged children."
"The policy was designed to support less privileged communities."

Underprivileged is almost always used with sympathy and concern. It is a softer, more compassionate word than saying someone is "poor" or "disadvantaged."

Here is a simple way to remember the full range of this word:

  • When it describes a person's background or life circumstances, it means they have had more advantages than most, often unearned.
  • When it describes access or membership, it means specially authorized.
  • When it describes information or communication, it means legally protected from disclosure.
  • When it is used personally and emotionally — "I feel privileged" — it means deeply honored and fortunate.

The common thread running through all four senses is the same: not everyone has it. Whatever is "privileged" — whether a person, a document, a feeling, or an access level — is set apart from the ordinary, holding something that most others don't.
12767:
When you are privy to something, you have been let into the knowledge of something that is private, secret, or restricted — something that most other people don't know about or don't have access to.

Think of it this way: imagine a closed room where a small group of people are discussing something confidential. If you are allowed inside that room, you are privy to that conversation. If you are kept outside, you are not privy to it.

That's the heart of the word.

This is very important: as an adjective, "privy" almost never stands alone. It virtually always appears in the phrase "privy to [something]." You are privy to a secret, privy to a plan, privy to information. The word "to" is its constant companion.

You would not say "She is privy" and stop there. You would say "She is privy to the decision."

"Privy to" carries a few quiet but important ideas packed inside it:

1. Exclusivity — not everyone knows.
The thing you are privy to is not public knowledge. It is held by a select few. The moment something becomes known to everyone, the word "privy" no longer applies naturally.

2. Access was granted or happened by circumstance.
Being privy to something means you were either deliberately included — someone trusted you enough to let you in — or you happened to be in a position where you came to know it. Either way, there's a sense of being inside a private circle, as opposed to being an outsider.

3. It describes your relationship to the information, not the information itself.
The secret is the secret. But "privy" describes you — specifically, that you have access to it. Two different people can be in two different states relative to the same secret: one is privy to it, the other is not.

These examples will show you how naturally "privy to" fits into everyday and formal contexts:

  • "Only three people in the company were privy to the merger plan before it was announced."
    → The merger plan was confidential. Those three people had access to that confidential knowledge.
  • "As the CEO's personal assistant, she was privy to many sensitive conversations."
    → Her role placed her inside the circle of private information.
  • "He felt left out because he wasn't privy to what the group had decided."
    → The decision was made without including him in the knowledge loop.
  • "The journalist claimed to be privy to classified documents."
    → She had access to documents that were restricted and not meant for the general public.
  • "Are you privy to the details of their agreement?"
    → Do you know the private details, or are you on the outside?
  • "Not everyone in the department was privy to the budget figures."
    → Some people were kept out of that knowledge intentionally.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Privy" is a formal word. You will encounter it more in writing — journalism, legal documents, literature, business communication — than in casual everyday speech. In informal conversation, people are more likely to say "in the know," "clued in," or simply "I knew about it."

However, "privy to" is not so stiff that it feels out of place in everyday serious conversation. Someone might naturally say, "I wasn't privy to that" in a professional meeting or a thoughtful discussion without sounding unnatural.

The word also carries a neutral tone. It doesn't tell you whether being privy to something is good or bad — that depends entirely on what the secret or private information is. Being privy to a surprise party plan is delightful. Being privy to a crime is troubling. The word itself doesn't judge; it simply describes the state of access.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what "privy to" does not mean:

  • It does not mean you agree with something. You can be privy to a plan and completely oppose it.
  • It does not mean you caused or created the information. You simply have access to it.
  • It does not mean you will share the information. Being privy to a secret says nothing about whether you'll keep it or reveal it.
  • It does not apply to general public knowledge. If something is widely known, no one is meaningfully "privy" to it — the exclusivity is gone.

Whenever you see or want to use "privy to," ask yourself: "Is this person inside the circle of private knowledge, or outside it?"

If inside → privy to it.
If outside → not privy to it.

That's the whole word.
12768: A prize is something desirable that you get as a result of winning, competing, or being exceptionally lucky or skilled. It is something that doesn't just come to you freely — there is an element of earning it, winning it, or capturing it.
Meaning 1 — Something Won in a Competition or Contest

This is the most common and familiar meaning. A prize is the reward given to the winner (or sometimes runners-up) of a competition, contest, race, game, lottery, quiz, or any other event where people compete.

The prize can take many forms:

  • Money — "The chess tournament offers a prize of ₹5 lakh to the winner."
  • A physical object — a trophy, a medal, a certificate, a car, a gadget.
  • An experience — a vacation, tickets to an event.

The key idea is that the prize is given specifically because someone won or performed exceptionally well. It is not given out of generosity alone — it is earned through performance.

Examples:

  • "She trained for months and finally won the first prize at the national dance competition."
  • "The prize for guessing the correct number was a brand-new bicycle."
  • "He entered the lucky draw and walked away with the top prize — a trip to Europe."

Notice that a prize can be awarded in a skill-based competition (like a debate or a race) or a luck-based one (like a lottery or a raffle). Both are valid uses. What unites them is the idea of something awarded to someone who "wins."

Important nuance — grades of prizes:
Competitions often have more than one prize. The best performance wins the first prize (also called the top prize or grand prize), and lesser performances may win second prize, third prize, and so on. At the very bottom, a booby prize is a humorous, mock award given to the person who performed worst — it's meant as a joke, not a real honor.

Named, prestigious prizes:
Some prizes are so famous they have become institutions in themselves. These are formal prizes given annually or periodically to honor outstanding achievement in a field:

  • The Nobel Prize — awarded for exceptional contributions to science, literature, or peace.
  • The Pulitzer Prize — awarded for excellence in journalism and literature.
  • The Booker Prize — awarded for the best novel written in English.

These are still "prizes" in the same sense — they are awarded because someone won recognition through their outstanding work.
Meaning 2 — Something (or Someone) of Exceptional Value or Desirability

Outside of formal competitions, "prize" is also used as a noun to refer to anything — or anyone — considered extremely valuable, rare, desirable, or worth having. Here, the idea of a competition is gone, but the idea of something being especially worth having remains.

Examples:

  • "That antique vase is a real prize — you won't find another like it anywhere."
  • "Investors consider that startup a prize acquisition."
  • "In the job market, a candidate fluent in four languages is quite a prize."
  • "He finally found the painting he had been hunting for years — a genuine prize."

In this sense, calling something a "prize" means it is not ordinary. It is something that stands out, something that people would compete to have if they could. The word carries a feeling of "this is special, this is rare, this deserves to be celebrated."

This meaning is also used for people. If someone refers to another person as "a prize," they typically mean that person is exceptionally talented, attractive, accomplished, or desirable in some way — someone others would be lucky to have as a partner, employee, or friend.
Meaning 3 — A Captured Ship or Cargo (Nautical / Historical Use)

This is a more specialized, historical meaning. In naval warfare and piracy, a prize refers to an enemy ship, vessel, or its cargo that has been captured at sea by an opposing force or privateer.

Examples:

  • "The warship sailed back to port with its prize — a captured merchant vessel loaded with silk and spices."
  • "Pirates in the 17th century grew rich from the prizes they seized in the Caribbean."

This meaning is rarely used in everyday modern conversation, but you will encounter it in historical texts, novels set at sea, or discussions of naval history. The underlying idea is the same — something won or seized through effort and conflict.

• Prize money — The cash given to the winner of a competition. "The boxing match had prize money of $2 million."
  • Grand prize — The biggest, most valuable prize in a competition. "She won the grand prize — a fully-paid scholarship."
  • First prize / Second prize / Third prize — Rankings in a competition. "He was disappointed to take only second prize after all his hard work."
  • Booby prize — A mock award for the worst performer, given humorously. "He came in last and received the booby prize — an alarm clock shaped like a rooster."
  • No prize for guessing — A common expression meaning the answer is so obvious that there is no reward needed for figuring it out. "No prize for guessing who ate the last piece of cake."
  • The prize is yours — A way of saying you have earned or deserved something.

These words are often confused because they overlap in meaning. Here is how they differ:

Prize vs. Award
Both are given for achievement. However, an award is almost always formal and institutional — like an award at a film festival or an award given by a professional organization. A prize can be formal or informal — you can win a prize at a school quiz just as you can win the Nobel Prize. Awards emphasize recognition; prizes emphasize winning and reward. In practice, the words are often used interchangeably for formal recognition.

Prize vs. Reward
A reward is given for any helpful action, service, or achievement — it doesn't require a competition. You might get a reward for returning a lost wallet. You wouldn't call that a prize. A prize specifically involves winning something — a contest, a race, a lottery, or being the best at something.

Prize vs. Gift
A gift is freely given out of kindness, affection, or generosity. You do nothing to "earn" a gift. A prize, on the other hand, is earned — through winning, competing, or being exceptionally valuable. If someone simply hands you money because they like you, that's a gift. If they hand you money because you won a competition, that's a prize.

Prize vs. Trophy
A trophy is a type of prize — specifically a physical object (usually a cup, shield, or figurine) that symbolizes victory. All trophies are prizes, but not all prizes are trophies. A prize can be money, an experience, or an object that is not a trophy.

No matter which meaning of "prize" you encounter, one idea runs through all of them:

A prize is not ordinary. It is something set apart — won, captured, or recognized as exceptional — and therefore especially worth having.

Whether it is a gold medal, a captured ship, or a rare gem described as "a real prize," the word always signals: this is something above the rest.
12769:
When the word pro bono describes something — a piece of work, a service, a case, a project — it means that professional work is being done completely free of charge, as an act of public service, for someone who cannot afford to pay for it.

The key word here is professional. Pro bono does not mean something is simply "free" in the everyday sense. It specifically means that a skilled, trained expert — someone who normally charges money for their expertise — is voluntarily giving that expertise away at no cost to the person receiving it.
The Three Pillars of Pro Bono Work

To call something truly pro bono, three things must be true at the same time:

  1. It involves professional skill. It is not just an act of kindness or a simple favour. It is expert work — the kind that requires years of training and that professionals charge significant fees for in the normal world.
  2. It is done for free. No fee, no payment, no barter, no "reduced rate." Zero.
  3. It serves a public good. The recipient is usually someone who cannot afford the service, or an organisation that works for the benefit of society. The spirit of pro bono is that skilled people use their abilities to serve those who would otherwise go without help.
Where You Will See It Most

The word is used most heavily in law. Lawyers and law firms are practically expected to take on some pro bono cases — meaning they represent clients who cannot afford legal fees. A poor person who needs a lawyer to fight a wrongful eviction, or an asylum seeker who needs help with immigration paperwork, might receive a pro bono legal defence — a full-quality legal service, at no cost to them.

But the word reaches far beyond law:

  • A pro bono accounting service might help a small charity organise its finances for free.
  • A pro bono medical consultation might be offered by a doctor to patients at a free clinic.
  • A pro bono design project might mean a graphic designer creates a logo and branding materials free of charge for a nonprofit organisation.
  • A pro bono consulting engagement might mean a business strategist helps a social enterprise plan its growth at no cost.

In every case, the shape is the same: an expert, giving real, high-quality professional work, free of charge, to help someone who needs it.

Understanding the boundaries of the word is just as important as knowing its meaning.

It is not a discount. If a lawyer charges you half their usual fee because you seem like a nice person, that is a discount. It is not pro bono. Pro bono means the cost is zero.

It is not charity in the general sense. A wealthy person donating money to a hospital is an act of charity. Pro bono specifically refers to the donation of professional skill and time, not money or goods.

It is not unpaid internship work or training. When a junior professional works for free to gain experience, that is not pro bono — they are the ones benefiting from the arrangement, not the recipient.

It is not volunteering in the casual sense. Anyone can volunteer at a food bank without any specific expertise. Pro bono work is different because it draws on specialised professional knowledge that the recipient could not otherwise access or afford.

Pro bono work carries a quiet but important moral weight. The idea behind it is that people who have built valuable professional skills have a responsibility — or at least a strong reason — to use those skills to help those who cannot afford them. Access to legal help, medical advice, financial guidance, and other professional services can completely change the outcome of a person's life. Without pro bono work, those services would simply be unavailable to anyone who cannot pay for them.

This is why, in law especially, many professional organisations and bar associations expect their members to contribute a certain number of pro bono hours each year. It is considered part of what it means to be a responsible professional.
How the Adjective Works in a Sentence

As an adjective, "pro bono" always describes a noun — the thing being done for free.

  • "She took on a pro bono case for a refugee family." — The case is being handled at no charge.
  • "The firm offers pro bono services to nonprofits." — The services are free.
  • "It was a pro bono project for a local school." — The project was done without payment.
  • "He spent twenty hours on pro bono work last month." — The work was unpaid professional service.

Notice that in every sentence, the word tells you the nature of the work arrangement — who pays (nobody) and why (public benefit).

Pro bono (adjective) describes professional work — legal, medical, financial, creative, or otherwise — that is done completely free of charge as a service to people who cannot afford it or to society at large. It is not a vague synonym for "free." It is specific: expert skill, voluntarily given, at zero cost, for the public good.
